Okay, I fully expect to get called a SJW for this, but for the record I'm coming at this from a linguistics perspective. One, everything is semantic bullshit. Words mean things--that's the point. Their semantic content is socially, culturally, and contextually determined. In South Africa, "colored" is an accepted demographic category (it's used to describe people of mixed race). In the US, "colored" was used by a bunch of racist motherfuckers tryna fuck black people over; when you call someone colored in the US, that's what you're invoking. It's retarded to pretend otherwise by pointing to a dictionary and saying, "Well, Merriam-Webster says it means either 'a quality such as red, blue, green, yellow, etc., that you see when you look at something' or 'the use or combination of colors'!", just like it's retarded to say "Stop being so pissy, they say colored in South Africa all the time!" Calling someone colored is an insult, so people get insulted.

Okay, so, that rant's finished. As far as OP's question goes, here's my theory: yes, it's more racist, and it assumes that white is the default, that's the point. Broadly speaking, minorities in the US face discrimination at individual and structural levels; like it or not, white people tend not to face racial discrimination that's so entrenched or institutionalized (yes, I realize there are many anecdotal exceptions, regional variations, whatever). I would guess that the term "people of color" is trying to capture the experience of marginalization shared by racial/ethnic minority communities--an experience which is deliberately defined in contrast to that of "white America" or whatever. Basically, the term seems racist because it mainly has meaning as an acknowledgment of racial inequities.

Then again, I think people also use it in a more value-neutral way as a PC descriptor that (as OP implies) seems to be deliberately tip-toeing around racial issues, too, so I guess things are complicated and who the fuck knows? Maybe the appeal is that it *doesn't *actually assume white is the default, particularly compared to saying something like "non-white"?

DISCLAIMERS: I don't know, I'm just kind of spitballing--if I had to guess, that's what I'd guess. I'm not trying to say that plenty of white people don't have it hard, or that plenty of black/hispanic/whatever/peopleofcolor people don't have it great. This isn't an endorsement or criticism of any policy. I don't support the censoring of any words--but I do think we need to recognize that some shit is offensive, you know it's offensive, and if you say offensive shit, then be prepared for someone to be offended. Doesn't mean it's right for people to say "I'm so offended!" as a justification for censoring someone's free speech--just that you should take responsibility for what you say. But also, my preference is for people to be chill and be able to recognize when someone does and doesn't mean to be offensive, and if people are just kind of nice and respectful to each other then shit tends to work out. To be clear, I don't mean to suggest that either OP or @Chingasa has said anything offensive (though I still think it's stupid to act like people are being ridiculous if they prefer a designation that doesn't sound like it's straight out of Deliverance).

Important add-on: it's an attempt at "person-first language." The APA calls for the use of person-first language as they believe it's more respectful. You don't call people "schizophrenics," they're "people with schizophrenia," and so on.
